questions.q: The title "vHkh Hkh eqvutks&nM+ks vkSj gM+Iik izkphu" contains the word "izkphu". What does "izkphu" indicate about the nature of this text, and which TWO cities are being referenced?
questions.a: "izkphu" (ancient/former) indicates the text describes these cities as they existed historically, not in their present ruined state. The two cities are Fatehpur Sikri (eqvutks&nM+ks) — Akbar's capital near Agra — and Agra (gM+Iik) itself, the later Mughal capital. A wrong answer (e.g., "izkphu means 'old' without connecting to historical reconstruction, or naming Delhi instead of Agra) reveals the student cannot decode title-level semantic cues or lacks basic Mughal geography knowledge.

questions.q: The opening paragraph states: "Hkkjr osQ gh ugha] nqfu;k osQ nks lcls iqjkus fu;ksftr 'kgj ekus tkrs gSaA" (Not just in India, but counted among the two most magnificent cities in the world). Why does the author make this hyperbolic claim at the very start, and what narrative purpose does it serve?
questions.a: The hyperbole establishes the chapter's central tension: the contrast between past glory and present ruin. By claiming world-historical status, the author frames the subsequent architectural descriptions as evidence for a lost civilization's greatness, inviting the reader to measure the ruins against this benchmark. A student who answers "to make it sound interesting" misses the structural function — this is not mere decoration but a thesis statement that the rest of the text will substantiate through architectural detail.

questions.q: Analyze the phrase: "flaèkq ?kkVh lH;rk dk lcls cM+k 'kgj gh ugha Fkk] mls lkèkuksa vkSj O;oLFkkvksa dks ns[krs gq, lcls le`¼ Hkh ekuk x;k gSA" (Fatehpur Sikri was not just the largest city of Akbar's reign, but also the most planned when viewing its systems and arrangements). What specific urban planning evidence from the text supports the claim of "le`¼" (planned), and how does this contrast with typical medieval Indian cities?
questions.a: Evidence for "le`¼": (1) Grid-like "x<+" (ridge) layout with distinct zones — administrative (Diwan-i-Aam/Khas), residential (palaces on ridge), religious (Jama Masjid), commercial (bazaars along roads). (2) Uniform building materials (red sandstone) and proportional scaling. (3) Integrated water management (lake, wells, drainage). (4) Social zoning — craftsmen quarters separated by trade, not caste. Contrast: Medieval Indian cities typically grew organically around a fort/temple with mixed-use, irregular lanes, caste-based segregation, and no master plan. A student citing only "wide roads" misses the systemic zoning evidence; one claiming "Mughal cities were always planned" overgeneralizes — Shahjahanabad (Delhi) was far less planned.
